SK2082 The collection element is written twice with nothing reading it in between

One entry of a list, array or dictionary is assigned twice in a contiguous run of element writes, so the first value is computed and thrown away.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since1.3
SupersedesS4143

Why

A block of map[…] = …; statements is how a lookup table gets built by hand, and it is where one key gets written twice: the first value is computed, stored and discarded by a later statement, and nothing in the compiler notices because both writes are legal. Either a key is wrong or a line is redundant, and which of the two it is decides what the program was supposed to do — which is also why there is no fix.

Example

Instead of:

limits["read"] = 100;
limits["write"] = 50;
limits["read"] = 25;

Write:

limits["read"] = 100;
limits["write"] = 50;
limits["admin"] = 25;

When it does not fire

⚠ Roslyn's `AnalyzeDataFlow` answers questions about variables, not about indexed elements, so there is no dataflow behind this rule and it does not pretend to have any. It reports only a contiguous run of element writes to one collection: the moment a statement that is not such a write appears between the two, the finding is withdrawn. That is a fraction of the defect and it is the fraction that can be proved without a lattice — a loop, a branch, a method call or a ref escape between the writes all end the run. ⚠ The run is additionally required to be opaque-free: an invocation, an object creation, an await, a lambda, a nested assignment, a ++ or a ref argument anywhere in an intervening write ends it, and so does any mention of the collection itself on the right of one, because each is a place the first value could be read through an alias. ⚠ "The keys are different" is a stronger claim than "the keys are not the same", and only two constants answer it. Two variables may hold one value and a comparer may make two distinct-looking values one key, so an undecidable pair ends the run rather than being stepped over. Two keys are the same when they are equal constants — which every IEqualityComparer<T> agrees with, since equality is reflexive — or when they are one storage read twice. ⚠ `ConcurrentDictionary` is not in the receiver table, deliberately: the point of the type is that another thread may read between the two writes, so "nothing read it" is not something this analysis is entitled to say there. The receiver must be an array or one of List<T>, Dictionary<K, V>, SortedDictionary<K, V> or SortedList<K, V>; a user type's indexer setter may accumulate, log or dispatch, and two writes to one index there are two events rather than one lost value. Compound assignment (c[k] += v) is a read as well as a write and is never a candidate.
